newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenian leaders pledge tax cuts, halt right.
newsitem.headline: Slovenian leaders pledge tax cuts, halt right.

text.p: Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek vowed on Thursday to halt an alliance of rightist parties from securing power in Sunday's general election, while his finance minister pledged tax cuts for the low-paid.
Victory by an electoral alliance set up by the People's Party, conservative Christian Democrats and centre-right Social Democrats would shift Slovenia sharply to the right.

The alliance, which calls itself the "Slovenian Spring", hopes to win more than 50 percent of the vote but have an uphill battle to oust Drnovsek's centre-left Liberal Democrats, currently riding high in opinion polls.
"The Liberal Democrats are offering the only serious alternative to the appearance of the three "Spring' parties," Drnovsek told the daily Dnevnik.
Sunday's general election is the second in Slovenia since independence from former Yugoslavia in 1991.
Drnovsek, who has led a fragile coalition government since the last election in 1992, accused all three parties of looking too much to the past instead of mapping out a secure future for Slovenia.
Finance Minister Mitja Gaspari told a news conference a new Liberal Democrat-led government would cut income tax for most low-paid workers, but gave no further details.

He shrugged off opposition criticism over higher public spending this year, which he said had risen 21.8 percent. Most of the increase was due to higher wages awarded in the public sector following a series of strikes, he said.

Labour unrest has marred Slovenia's economic record, one of the best among ex-communist states. Growth last year rose 3.5 percent after contracting 9.3 percent in 1991 when Slovenia seceded from the former Yugoslav federation.
The healthy economy has contributed in part to growing support for Drnovsek's Liberal Democrats of up to 22 percent, with the People's Party in second place at around 10 percent.
Drnovsek will probably have to rely on a partnership with one or two rightist parties to form a new government, but the premier wants his centre-left party to remain dominant.
Most political parties are committed to developing a free market in Slovenia and little separates the main players in their support for membership of NATO and the European Union.

But the People's Party argues that EU entry should only be agreed with full guarantees to protect the farming sector. The party's main backing comes from farmers and farm workers, who make up a hefty 20 percent of the national work force.
The Christian Democrats have pledged to fight for the restoration of land and property to the Roman Catholic church, dispossessed when communists took power after World War Two.

The United List party, the former communists, has the backing of labour unions, worried about the rising jobless rate at 13.5 percent. But opinion polls show support for the United List at only about six percent.
